item.title: Iruka 1.1.8.0
item.description:
The One With the Diff Pane and the Folder Sizes

Added

  • The setup for SFTP, FTP and cloud mounts is now spelled out as three steps, everywhere. Mounting needs the official rclone and a FUSE layer, and the connection dialog used to name only the single next thing missing — so you ran the install line, hit a fresh warning about fuse-t, and never found out that the uninstall standing in front of it was why your install had silently done nothing at all. Homebrew's rclone can't mount, and while it is there the official installer sees the same version and skips. The warning in the dialog now lists all three steps every time, in order and numbered: remove Homebrew's rclone, install the official one from rclone.org, install fuse-t. Each one says what it is for, shows its exact command with its own copy button, and is ticked off, struck through or marked skip this according to what's already on your Mac — with Copy remaining for everything still to run. The docs are written the same way, so what you read on the site and what the app tells you are the same three numbered steps.
  • Copy a file's path, full or relative. Right-click anything — in the file list, the icon grid or a column — and there's Copy Full Path and Copy Relative Path. The relative one is measured from the git repository root when you're in a repository, which is the form you paste into a coding agent, an issue or a review and have it mean the same thing to everyone; outside a repository it's measured from the folder you're looking at. Inside a repository, when the folder you're in isn't the repository root, Copy Path Relative to This Folder is offered as well, so both readings are available and neither silently wins. Select several files and you get one path per line. Right-clicking empty space copies the folder's own path the same two ways.
  • Open in External Terminal. Right-click a folder — or empty space in the one you're browsing — and you can open it in a real terminal window. On a file the entry reads Open Containing Folder in External Terminal, since that's the only thing a terminal can be opened at. It starts the shell you chose in Settings → Terminal, so the outside window is the same shell as the pane inside Iruka rather than whatever the terminal app happens to default to. Settings → Terminal has a new External terminal picker listing the terminal apps you actually have installed — Terminal, iTerm, Ghostty, WezTerm, kitty, Alacritty, Warp and others — defaulting to Terminal. (The shell is imposed for Terminal and iTerm; the others get the folder and use their own configured shell.)
  • The path bar's folder icon is now a way up. Click it and the whole path drops down as a vertical list — the folder you're in at the top, everything above it below — so any ancestor is one click away instead of a ⌘↑ per level or a hand-edited path. Clicking the path text still puts you in edit mode exactly as before, and the pencil is unchanged.
  • An optional breadcrumb bar. View → Show Breadcrumb Bar puts a row of clickable folders under the path bar — off by default, because the path bar is the established way around and this is a second one for people who prefer it. Every crumb navigates, and the › between two crumbs lists that folder's subfolders, so you can step sideways into a sibling without going up and back down. A deep path scrolls, keeping the folder you're actually in on screen.
  • The preview pane tells you about the file, not just shows it. Under every preview there's now a collapsible Info strip with the things you'd otherwise open Get Info for: kind, exact size in bytes, created and modified dates, owner and group, permissions in both rwxr-xr-x and octal, where it lives, and — where they apply — an image's pixel dimensions, an application's version and bundle identifier, and what a symlink points at. Everything is selectable text, so you can copy any of it. Click Info to fold it away; the choice sticks across tabs, windows and relaunches.
  • Folders get a real preview instead of a giant icon. Selecting a folder used to fill the preview pane with a 128-point folder icon, which told you nothing you didn't already know. Now you get a small icon, the name, what the folder contains at the top level (12 folders, 340 files), and its recursive size once that's been worked out — along with all the dates and permissions above.
  • How much a folder actually holds — in the Size column, in the status bar, and in the preview pane, from one measurement rather than three. Nothing on disk records a folder's size, so it has to be walked: one folder at a time, in the background, below everything else, dropped the moment its answer stops being wanted, and giving up on anything enormous with a ≥ 4.2 GB rather than pretending. Select things and the status bar totals them, folders included; select nothing and it tells you how much is in the folder you're looking at — worked out last of all, so it never delays the rows in front of you. Applications are measured too, so how big is this app finally has an answer. Turn the whole thing off in Settings → General → Folder sizes; the preview pane keeps a Calculate button either way.
  • Sort folders in among the files, if you want to. Folders have always been pinned above files, which quietly meant that sorting by Date Modified ordered the folders among themselves and the files among themselves and answered nobody's question — what changed most recently in here had two answers and neither was on top. Settings → General → Sorting → Keep folders on top when sorting (on by default) turns the pin off, and then every column sorts everything together, in the list, the icon grid and the columns. Sorting by size with folders unpinned uses each folder's measured size, since a folder has no size of its own to sort by.
  • Advanced Search is a window now, not a sheet. You can move it, resize it, put it beside the folder you're searching, and carry on using the file list while a search that takes a minute runs — none of which a sheet allows, since a sheet is nailed to the top of its window and blocks it. It remembers where you left it, and reopening it while it's already up just brings it forward pointed at the folder you're in.
  • PDFs zoom. The preview pane showed PDFs through Quick Look, which renders them well and gives you no way to make them bigger — no controls, and ⌘= did nothing. A PDF is a page laid out for paper being shown in a pane a third of a window wide, so it's the one preview where zoom is the point. PDFs now get the same −/100%/+ control and the same ⌘−, ⌘= and ⌘0 as the text previews, with 100% meaning fit-to-width.
  • Zoomed images and SVGs can be dragged around, and keep their scroll bars. Panning a zoomed preview needed a two-finger scroll, and the scroll bars faded out a second after you stopped — which is exactly when you want to see which part of the picture you're looking at. Grab it and drag now, with the hand cursor to say so, and the scroll bars stay put while you're zoomed in. The wheel and two-finger scrolling work as before.
  • ssh keys work for push and pull however your agent is set up. Launched from Finder, Iruka inherits none of your shell's environment — so on a machine where the agent is registered with launchd, or where 1Password rather than your .zshrc provides it, git push to a private ssh remote failed with Permission denied (publickey) while the agent was running and the key was loaded the whole time. Iruka now finds the agent the same way it already did for SFTP mounts, before anything needs it. It still holds no keys, passphrases or tokens of its own: prompts belong in the terminal and GitHub belongs to gh.
  • The status strip says when a merge or rebase is unfinished. A repository left half-way through a merge, rebase, cherry-pick, revert or bisect — which is the state a coding agent leaves one in constantly — used to look exactly like a clean checkout: a branch name, a count of changed files, and a Commit button that would have baked the half-applied state in as a commit of its own. There's now a red MERGING / REBASING / CHERRY-PICKING pill beside the branch name, and hovering it tells you which command finishes the job (git rebase --continue, git merge --abort, and so on). It's read from git's own state, so it appears and disappears exactly when git thinks so — including inside a linked worktree.
  • Swap the two sides of a comparison. The ⇄ between the two names in the diff pane's header is now a button for file and folder comparisons: which folder lands on the left is decided by path order, or by which pane it came from, and neither is what you meant if you wanted it the other way round. Git comparisons keep it as a label — there the left side is a commit and the right is your working tree, and swapping those would claim your edits are what you're comparing against.
  • The changed-file count opens the review. The ● 12 beside your branch is the thing everyone looks at to ask "what changed", and it did nothing; the Review button was one word among six in a strip that truncates in a narrow pane. The count is now a button with an eye on it, and it replaces the Review button — it's shown exactly when there is something to review, which is when Review was enabled anyway. ⇧⌘U, the right-click menu entry and the Diff button are all unchanged.
  • Start a git repository from the folder you're looking at. Right-click empty space in any folder that isn't already in a repository and there's Initialize Git Repository Here…. It asks first and shows you the full path, because git init in the wrong folder — your home directory, the root of a synced folder — is the sort of mistake that stays quiet for weeks. If the folder turns out to be inside a repository already, it says which one and does nothing, so you can't end up with a repository nested inside another without knowing.
  • Add Remote… — a new button in the status bar of any repository that hasn't got one. This closes a dead end: until now a repository you'd just created could commit and then had nowhere to send anything, and the Push button never appeared at all. Give it a URL and Push turns up as soon as you've made a commit — the first push sets the branch tracking automatically. A freshly initialised repository now also shows its real branch name rather than "HEAD", and no longer offers a Push that couldn't have worked.
  • Fetch. The ahead and behind counts beside your branch name are only ever as honest as your last fetch, and nothing in Iruka ever performed one — so a repository could sit there confidently reporting nothing to pull for a week. There's now a Fetch button whenever the repository has a remote. It runs in the terminal pane, so a passphrase prompt has somewhere to appear, and the counts catch up on their own afterwards.
  • Discard a file's changes. Right-click a modified file — in the file list, the icon grid, the column browser, or a row in the review pane — and choose Discard Changes… to put it back the way your last commit has it. It asks first, and the question tells you what you're actually losing: how many lines added and removed, that anything you've staged goes too, and that this one doesn't go to the Trash and can't be undone. Return cancels — the red button has to be clicked — because unstaging is one harmless click away in the same list and the two must never be reachable by the same reflex. Deleted a file by accident? The same entry reads Restore From Last Commit… there, isn't red, and simply brings it back. Files git has never seen aren't offered any of this: for those, Move to Trash is a few lines up the same menu and you can get them back.
  • Create a pull request. If you have GitHub's gh installed and logged in, a repository on a pushed branch gets a Pull Request button that opens the new-PR page in your browser, filled in for that branch. It's a handoff, like the FileMerge button — Iruka doesn't try to be a pull-request client — and it isn't shown at all unless gh is there and authenticated, so it's never a button that can't work.
  • Unstage from the right-click menu. You could stage a file from the file list and then had no way to take it back out without opening the review pane — which you had to know was there. Unstage now sits next to Stage. It only ever changes what the next commit would record; your edits aren't touched.
  • Compare two folders. Select two folders and choose Compare — from the right-click menu or ⇧⌘C — and the diff pane lists everything that differs between them: what's only on the left, what's only on the right, and what's in both but changed. In dual-pane mode, press ⇧⌘C with nothing selected and it compares the two folders you're looking at, which is the question two panes exist to answer; or select one folder in each pane and compare those. Each changed file shows how many lines it gained and lost — +35 −24 — so you can see which ones are worth opening before you open any of them; those fill in just after the list appears, since counting them means actually reading both copies. Pick any changed file in the list and its diff appears beside it, exactly as a review does — ⌥↑ and ⌥↓ step through, and the file list keeps its own ↑/↓ throughout. This is how you answer "what's different between this and the backup?", or check what an agent changed in a directory that isn't a repository. The comparison only ever tells you — there is no button anywhere in it that copies, moves or deletes anything. Results stream in as the folders are walked, so a comparison of two large trees is readable and clickable within moments rather than after a spinner, and there's a Stop button that keeps everything found so far. Files are compared by size, and where the sizes match but the timestamps don't, by their actual contents — so a file that was merely touched, rebuilt or copied doesn't get reported as changed. A folder the other side hasn't got is listed once, as itself, rather than as a thousand rows for everything inside it. Symbolic links are compared as links and never followed, so a link pointing back up its own tree can't send the comparison round in circles. .git is skipped on both sides, since repository internals differ between any two clones for reasons that aren't your work — the pane says so when it happens. On a network or FUSE mount, where reading every file would mean downloading it and timestamps can't be trusted, the comparison uses sizes alone and tells you it did, rather than quietly being less thorough than it looks. Folders it couldn't read are reported too.
  • The diff pane has its own zoom. ⌘= and ⌘− now resize the diff and the list of files beside it, with buttons in the pane's header and ⌘0 to reset. They only worked while a text preview happened to be open before, so the way to make a diff readable was to open a preview first and zoom that.
  • The review keeps up with an agent while you watch it work. Leave the review pane open while a coding agent, a build or a script changes files, and the list now catches up on its own — before, it only noticed when you left Iruka and came back, so a repository being rewritten beside you could sit there apparently unchanged. It checks more often on small repositories and backs off on large ones, so it never becomes the thing slowing you down, and it stops entirely while Iruka is in the background. ⌘R refreshes it immediately, as does the ↻ button.
  • Build a commit out of exactly the files you want, without leaving the review. Every row in the review list has a checkbox for whether the next commit will include it, and there's a Commit… button right there once anything is ticked — it opens with Stage all changes already off, so what you picked is what you get. The checkbox at the top of the list ticks or unticks everything at once. Unticking only takes a file back out of the staging area; your edits are never touched. This is what makes the review useful for splitting an agent's work into sensible commits rather than only reading it.
  • Files you staged and then edited again show as half-ticked. A dash instead of a tick, because a commit would record the earlier version of that file and leave your newer edits behind — which is worth knowing before you commit rather than after. Clicking stages the rest.
  • Staging and committing now work from anywhere. Stage File, Stage All Changes and Commit were sent to the terminal pane, and were quietly dropped unless the main browser window happened to be frontmost — so from a second window they did nothing at all, with the badge still showing the file as modified and no commit made. All three now run directly and tell you if git refuses; if a pre-commit hook rejects the commit, the sheet stays open with your message intact and shows you what the hook said. Push and pull still go through the terminal, where a password prompt needs somewhere to appear.
  • Review everything you changed, file by file. In a git repository, click Review in the status bar — or press ⇧⌘U — and the diff pane fills with every file that differs from your last commit: the changed paths listed down one side, the diff of whichever one you pick on the other. This is the quickest way to read back what a coding agent has just done to a repository before you commit it, which is what the whole Compare feature was built for. Files git has never seen are included, shown in full as additions — those are usually exactly the files that were just created, and a plain git diff says nothing at all about them. Deleted files are there too. Step through with ⌥↑ and ⌥↓, or click; the file list keeps its own ↑/↓ throughout, so nothing changes about arrowing through your folders. Drag the divider inside the pane to give the list or the diff more room. Commit, and the review catches up on its own; come back to Iruka after working elsewhere and it looks again, keeping you on the file you were reading. Each changed file shows how many lines it gained and lost — +35 −24 — so you can see which ones are worth opening before you open any of them. The Diff button still compares a single selected file with HEAD as before — with nothing selected it now offers the whole review instead of sitting there disabled. You can also start a review by right-clicking empty space in a folder: when there's anything uncommitted, the menu offers it along with the count, so you don't have to remember the shortcut or find the button.
  • Look inside an app. Right-click an application — or any bundle, like a .mdimporter or a .photoslibrary — and choose Show Package Contents to browse what's in it, the way you would any other folder. Double-clicking still launches the app, as it should; this is the deliberate way in, for when you want an Info.plist, a bundled resource, or just to see how something is put together. Available in list, icon and column views, and once you're inside, everything works as normal — navigating, previewing, and going back out.
  • Compare two files, or one file against your last commit. Select two files and choose Compare — from the right-click menu or ⌘⇧C — and a diff pane opens on the right showing exactly what differs, line by line, additions in green and removals in red. Select a single file inside a git repository and the same command shows what you've changed since your last commit, which is the quickest way to read back what an AI coding agent just did to a file before you commit it. The older file is always on the left, so a diff reads the way you'd describe it: before on one side, after on the other. It's a pane of its own, next to the file list and independent of the preview pane, so you can have the folder, a preview and a diff on screen at once — and nothing pops up in front of what you were doing. Drag its edge to resize it, and close it with the ✕ in its corner — it opens only when you ask for it, and stays put while you carry on browsing, switching tabs or moving between panes. In a git repository there's also a Diff button beside Commit in the status bar: select a file, click it, and you're looking at what you changed. In dual-pane mode, select one file in each pane and Compare puts them side by side — the obvious question to ask of two panes, and it works whether or not either folder is a repository. Where more than one comparison makes sense the menu offers all of them, so two selected files in a repository can be compared with each other or each with its committed version. Changed lines get a coloured band across the whole width, and when only part of a line changed, the words that differ are picked out in a stronger shade — so a one-character fix doesn't look like a whole rewritten line. Lines that were replaced outright are left plainly coloured rather than speckled. Files that turn out to be identical say so plainly rather than showing you an empty page, and images, archives and other binary files say they differ instead of pretending to be text. If you have Xcode's tools installed there's a button to hand the same two files to FileMerge when you want to edit or merge rather than read — including for a comparison against a commit, where Iruka writes out the committed version for you.
  • Checksums in the right-click menu. Checksum… on any selection now shows SHA-256 and MD5 with a button to copy either — for verifying a download against a published hash, or confirming a file survived a transfer intact. Pick exactly two files and it also answers the question directly: identical, or different. That answer comes from comparing the files' contents rather than hashing them both to the end, so on two large files that differ early it comes back immediately.

Fixed

  • Scrolling a large folder is smooth again. Every row was quietly building its entire right-click menu — the list of applications that can open the file, the git entries, the compare targets, the colour swatches — over and over as you scrolled, for menus nobody had opened. On a 1,700-entry folder that came to more than fifty thousand rebuilds a minute. They're built when you right-click now, which is the only moment they were ever looked at.
  • Switching tabs no longer re-reads the folder. Coming back to a tab re-enumerated, rebuilt and re-sorted a folder that was already on screen, twice over, with the window stalled behind it. It's read once now, and only when it's genuinely out of date — the folder watcher keeps inactive tabs current, which is what made the reload redundant to begin with. A filter you'd typed also survives switching away and back, instead of being cleared.
  • Rubber-band selection is quick, and picks the rows you dragged over. Dragging a selection box through a large folder rebuilt the whole listing and tested every row against the box on every frame, which made it crawl. And with folders sorted in among the files, a folder size arriving mid-drag reordered the list under the pointer, so the selection came out shifted by a row at each end. The box works against the rows as they were when you started dragging, and reordering waits until you let go.
  • Dropping into the folder you're already looking at works. Dragging files out of the drop stack onto a folder worked; dropping them into the listing you were already in did nothing at all, unless you happened to hit the empty space below the last row — every file row was accepting the drop and then discarding it. A drop on a file row now means put it in this folder, which is what it looks like.
  • ↑ and ↓ in the path bar walk the completion list. They used to rewrite the field with the highlighted path, which made them a second Tab: what you'd typed was gone, so arrowing one past the entry you wanted and back left you unable to carry on typing. They move the highlight and nothing else now. Return goes to the highlighted entry, Tab still fills it in, Escape still gets you out.
  • Commit… is no longer offered part-way through a rebase. Committing there makes an ordinary commit that the rebase then carries straight past — the command that finishes the job is git rebase --continue, and the button now says so instead of being clickable. Same for a cherry-pick, a revert and a bisect. A merge keeps its Commit button, because a merge really does end in one.
  • Reveal in File List waits for the folder to load. It navigated, waited a fixed fraction of a second and then selected the file — which on a large folder, or one on a network mount, is before the listing has arrived, so the selection was set against the previous folder and lost. It now waits for the file to actually appear, and scrolls to it.
  • **Staging a folder that contains a conflict refuses, as Stage All already did.** git add on a folder marks every unresolved conflict inside it resolved; that was still reachable for a folder whose badge didn't say it held one.
  • The review no longer changes to another repository on its own. Open a review, open a second one later in the same window, and the pane's own background refresh went on asking about the first repository and writing its files into the pane that said it was showing the second — every few seconds, with nothing touched. The refresh loop kept the repository it was started with while everything else in the pane moved on. It now restarts whenever the comparison changes, a listing that has been superseded is discarded rather than applied, and changing what the pane shows stops the listing that belonged to what it showed before. The status bar has the same guard: a git status for the folder you have just navigated away from can no longer publish its repository over the one you're looking at, which is what made ⇧⌘U occasionally open the wrong repository's review.
  • The diff pane says which repository it is showing. It belongs to the window and deliberately stays put while you browse, so a review is regularly of a repository some other tab is in — and the header said only "HEAD ↔ Working tree", which is true of every repository there has ever been. That's how a MERGING pill in the status bar and a REBASING notice in the review end up on screen together, both correct and describing different repositories. The repository's name is now in the header, next to the close button.
  • A folder with an empty .git in it is no longer treated as a repository. Iruka decided a folder was a repository if something called .git was there at all — and a sync client had left an empty .git directory behind in one, so the status strip, the review and the git menu entries all appeared and then every one of them failed with git's own not a git repository. A git directory has to have a HEAD in it now; worktrees and submodules, which use a .git file instead, are unaffected.
  • Pull works on branches that have diverged. Since git 2.27, plain git pull refuses to run at all when your branch and the remote have each moved on — it stops with Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches and does nothing — which is exactly the situation the button exists for. It now says which it means: a merge, unless you've configured pull.rebase or pull.ff yourself, in which case your setting is used untouched.
  • Pull is offered whenever your branch tracks a remote, not only when Iruka already knows you're behind. The behind-count comes from your last fetch, so on a branch someone else has pushed to it reads 0 — which is exactly the moment your push is rejected with fetch first and the button that fixes it wasn't on screen.
  • gh set up with GH_TOKEN in your shell profile is recognised. Launched from Finder, Iruka inherits no profile, so a gh authenticated that way — rather than with gh auth login — looked signed out and the Pull Request button said so. The token is read from your login shell when, and only when, gh has no stored login of its own; it is never stored, written or logged.
  • The Pull Request button believes you after gh auth login. Signing in happens in the terminal pane a few inches below the button — so there's no switching away and back, and Iruka went on answering from a detection made up to five minutes earlier: press the button, be told to sign in, sign in, press again, be told to sign in. It now re-asks gh whenever you refresh with ⌘R, whenever Iruka comes forward, and — the one that matters — before refusing, so the second press works whatever the strip still thinks.
  • Right-clicking a file in icon view selects the file you clicked. It highlighted something else — usually a couple of icons away from the pointer — while the menu that opened acted on the right file, so the highlight and the menu disagreed about what you were about to do. The review pane had the other half of the same bug: the second right-click in a row highlighted nothing, leaving the diff beside it showing the previous file. Both views now work out which row was clicked from where the click landed rather than from what the pointer had most recently hovered, which is not something that can be relied on at the moment a menu opens.
  • **The review's Stage All stays out of the way during a merge or rebase.** It was already hidden while a conflict was unresolved; it now also stays hidden for the rest of an unfinished operation, and the list shows what's going on and how many files are still to resolve.
  • Files with spaces or accents in their names now get git badges and git menu entries. my notes.txt or café.swift showed no colour badge, no Stage Changes and no Discard — silently, while every plain-ASCII file beside them worked — because git quotes those names when it lists them and Iruka was taking the quotes literally.
  • Merge conflicts are recognised properly, and can't be resolved by accident. Several kinds of conflict — both sides adding the same file, both deleting it, one side deleting what the other changed — were shown as ordinary added or modified files, complete with a Stage Changes entry and a staging checkbox. Staging a conflicted file is what tells git the conflict is resolved, so one click on something labelled "modified" could silently accept one side of a merge, conflict markers and all. Conflicted files are now marked as conflicts everywhere, have no checkbox, and aren't included by Stage All — which disappears entirely while a merge is unresolved, as does the commit sheet's Stage all changes first, since git add -A marks conflicts resolved rather than skipping them. Resolving a merge is still a thing to do in the terminal.
  • A repository with a lot of uncommitted changes no longer loses its badges. Past a few hundred changed files, reading git's status could stall indefinitely — no error, no spinner, just a status strip that never appeared, as though the folder weren't a repository at all.
  • The status strip catches up after a commit made from the review pane. It kept showing the old number of changed files, no Push button, and Review still enabled for a commit you had already made.
  • The first push uses your actual remote. If you'd named it anything other than origin, Push ran against a remote that didn't exist and failed.
  • Pull and Push wait long enough for a slow connection. Over a slow link, the strip gave up watching before the command finished, leaving the counts wrong and Push still offered for work already pushed.
  • Reviewing changes from a file's right-click menu starts on that file, the same as ⇧⌘U and the Review button already did.
  • The review keeps up in a linked worktree. Committing or switching branches in one never refreshed the list, because Iruka was watching for changes in a folder that doesn't exist there.
  • Switching to column view shows where you are. Open a folder several levels down and switch to column view, and you got a single column with nothing to its left — so ← did nothing and column view could only go deeper, which is the opposite of what it's for. The folders above are now open beside it, scrolled so the one you were in is the one you see, back as far as your home folder.
  • Columns keep their width. The last column used to stretch into whatever space was left, so a single column filled the whole pane and looked like list view — and opening anything inside it snapped that column back to normal width, moving everything you were reading. Columns are now a fixed width and the space to the right is simply room for the next one.
  • A selected folder keeps its contents open beside it. Arrowing from one folder down to the next closed the column showing what was inside it, then reopened it when you stepped in — so the whole chain jumped sideways and back for a single press. The column to the right now follows the selection as you move. Landing on a file still closes it, as it should: there's nothing there to describe.
  • ← steps up a column the first time you press it. After clicking a folder, or switching into column view, the arrow keys were steering one column to the right of the one whose selection was actually highlighted — so the first ← moved to where you already were and appeared to do nothing, working only from the second press. ← and → now act on the column the highlight is in, and ← then → returns you to the file you were on rather than the top of the folder.
  • The columns scroll back into view when they lose room. Opening the diff pane — or the preview pane, or resizing the window — squeezed the column area without moving the chain, so a deep chain was left parked halfway along with the folder you were working in off the right-hand edge.
  • → works straight after clicking a folder in column view. Clicking a folder opens its column and moves the keyboard there, but nothing in it was selected yet — so → did nothing until you pressed ↑ or ↓ first, making the arrow keys look like they only worked after each other. → now steps into the column you're already in.
  • You can see which column the keyboard is driving. Every column keeps its selection highlighted — that trail is what makes column view readable — but they all looked identical, so pressing ← appeared to do nothing at all: the parent was already lit and the child stayed lit. The column you're actually in now shows its selection in the accent colour and the others in grey, the way macOS distinguishes them everywhere else.
  • Clicking empty space clears the selection in list and column view. It always has in icon view; in the other two the space below the last row did nothing, so the only way to drop a selection was to select something else. In column view the columns to the right go too — they were only there to show what you had selected.
  • The FileMerge button appears when you have FileMerge. It never did — Iruka looked for it inside Xcode's developer directory, and current Xcode keeps it one level above that. It also now works when the Command Line Tools are the selected developer tools, which is the usual state even on a machine with Xcode, and where the handoff would previously have failed outright.
  • The git strip notices files edited outside Iruka. Change a file with an editor that writes in place — or with sed, or a coding agent — and the dirty count, the badges and the Commit button stayed as they were, because the folder watcher only sees files being created, deleted or renamed, not their contents changing. It now catches up when you come back to Iruka, and when a command finishes in the terminal pane, which is the case where you never left.
  • A folder inside a large git repository no longer freezes the app. Opening one — a repository with tens of thousands of files, especially inside a synced folder like Dropbox — could beachball Iruka in any view, over and over, because the folder kept changing under it. Reading git status was running on the same thread that draws the window, so the app simply stopped until it finished. It now runs out of the way, and the badges appear when they're ready. Repositories with more changed files than badges could usefully describe now show the count alone.
  • Clicking a folder in column view is as fast as arrowing into it. In a folder with a few thousand items a click could take half a second or more, while pressing → on the same folder was instant. Every click was scrolling the columns sideways to bring the new one into view — even when they all fitted on screen already and there was nothing to scroll — and working out where to scroll to meant laying out every item in the folder you had clicked in. It now only scrolls when the columns genuinely overflow.
  • Editing a cloud connection no longer wipes its saved key. The secret field always opened empty — it never loaded what was in your Keychain — and saving wrote that empty value straight over the stored key. So changing anything else about a connection, even just its name, silently destroyed the credential and left it failing to mount with nothing on screen to explain why. An untouched field now leaves the stored key alone, and the field says so rather than looking as though no key were saved. There's an eye button to check a key as you type it, and an explicit Remove stored key for when you do want it gone.
  • Widening the preview pane no longer pushes everything off the window. Dragging its edge left worked until the file list ran out of room, and then the whole layout slid right: the preview and diff panes went off the edge of the window, the terminal drifted right with them, and in list view the Date Modified and Size columns disappeared off the side. The file pane refused to shrink past what its columns needed and grew wider than the space it had, carrying everything to its right along with it. It now keeps to its width and clips, as the dual-pane layout already did.
  • A narrow window no longer squashes the last column or cuts off the diff pane. The preview and diff panes each insisted on their minimum width even when the window was too small to give it, so together they overran it: the column browser was crushed until the column you were working in showed as a stripe a few pixels wide, and the diff pane hung half off the right edge. The panes now give way instead, and when the columns do overflow the browser rests against its trailing edge so the column you just opened is the one you can see.
  • Selecting a file in column view clears the column beside it. Open a folder, then click a file in the same column, and the folder's contents stayed on screen to the right — describing something you were no longer pointing at. A file has nothing to show beside it, so that column now goes.
  • Extracting in column view selects what it made. The new folder is now selected and brought into view — both the row and, if it had scrolled off the side, the column holding it. Before, the archive you had just expanded stayed selected with nothing to show where its contents had gone.
  • Double-click works in column view. It never did: a double-click on a zip selected it twice instead of extracting it, and on any other file it did nothing at all. Double-clicking now opens — extracting archives, drilling into folders, and handing everything else to the app that owns it, the same as ↵ and ⌘↓ already did.
  • The columns follow the keyboard. Opening a folder with → or a double-click didn't bring the new column into view — only clicking one did — and ← stepped back into a column that could be off the left-hand edge, leaving you driving a selection you couldn't see until ↑ or ↓ happened to drag it back.
  • Refresh now reloads the columns too. ⌘R updated the git strip but left every column showing what it had before, because it reloaded the tab's own listing — which column view deliberately doesn't keep current and never displays.
  • Deleting in list view no longer throws the list around. The next item is selected, as before, but the list stays put. It was scrolling that row to the top of the pane — a row that was already on screen, right where you had been looking.
  • Deleting in column view moves the selection on, as it does everywhere else. Trashing or deleting left nothing selected, so pruning a folder with the preview pane open meant reaching for the mouse after every file. The selection now lands on the next item — or the one before, when you've deleted from the end — exactly as in list and icon views.
  • The back and forward buttons on a mouse now navigate. The side buttons move through the folders you've visited, as they do in Finder and in every browser — Iruka ignored them before, so you had to reach for ⌘[ and ⌘].
  • The git strip keeps up with what you just did. Committing left it still showing the changes it had committed, and no Push button appeared for the commit you'd just made — the strip was read back before the command had finished running. It now catches up on its own, including after a slow pre-commit hook. Push also appears on a branch you've never pushed, where it sets up tracking for you rather than failing; a repository with no remote at all still offers nothing, as it should.

Changed

  • Column view uses the whole width. When the columns didn't fill the pane, the leftover sat beside them as a blank strip that read as a broken empty panel — most obviously next to the preview pane. That space now goes to the deepest column, which is the one you're working in.
  • The cloud connection sheet is wider, and its fields look like fields. Endpoint URLs are routinely longer than the sheet was, and with no box around them a field read as its own label and a long value ran on with nothing showing it had overflowed. Every field now has a visible border, the endpoint is shown in a monospaced font, and the sheet is wide enough for a real URL.
  • One preview pane per window, in every view. Column view used to carry its own preview as a trailing column, which meant a dual-pane window in column view showed two previews — one per side. There is now a single preview pane on the right, showing whatever the active pane has selected, whichever view mode either side is in.
  • The git buttons are no longer tiny. Pull, Push, Commit… and Diff were small enough to read as status badges rather than things you can press. They're now a normal size with an icon beside each label, in the same place at the end of the status bar.

---

item.title: Iruka 1.1.7.2
item.description:
Added

  • “Open in Iruka” is now in Finder's own right-click menu. Right-click a folder — or the empty space inside the folder you're looking at — and Open in Iruka is there directly, no longer tucked away under the Services submenu. Select several folders and each opens in its own tab; right-click a file and you get the folder it lives in. The same item can go on Finder's toolbar as a button: right-click the toolbar, choose Customize Toolbar, and drag Iruka's icon up. macOS asks you to switch this on first — System Settings → General → Login Items & Extensions → Finder Extensions, then tick Iruka — and Settings → General → Finder Integration tells you whether it's on and takes you straight there. The Services item is still there for anyone who has given it a keyboard shortcut.

Fixed

  • The menu bar no longer has two menus called View. There were genuinely two, sitting a few menus apart and both carrying macOS's own Show Tab Bar and Enter Full Screen items, so which one held Icon View or Show Terminal was a coin toss. There is now one View menu with everything in it.

Changed

  • Copy to Other Pane and Move to Other Pane have moved into the Edit menu. They sit just below Duplicate, next to Copy and Paste where operations on the selection belong, instead of in a menu of their own holding two items. ⌥⌘C and ⌥⌘M still work, and so does any shortcut you assigned to them yourself — the commands are named exactly as before, only the menu they live in has changed.
  • Keyboard Shortcuts is listed once, under Help. It also appeared in the Window menu among Minimize and Zoom, so the same window was offered twice in two different places.

item.title: Iruka 1.1.7.1
item.description:
Added

  • Open a folder in Iruka from anywhere on the system. Right-clicking a folder in Finder now offers Services → Open in Iruka, and you can give that a keyboard shortcut under System Settings → Keyboard → Keyboard Shortcuts → Services — so a folder you're looking at in Finder is one keystroke away from an Iruka tab. Iruka also opens a folder handed to it by open -a Iruka some-folder in a terminal, by an iruka:// link such as iruka:///Users/you/Documents for scripts and automation, and by dropping a folder on its Dock icon. If Iruka isn't running, it launches and opens the folder; if it is, the folder arrives as a new tab. There's a Settings → General → Finder Integration section collecting all of this. What macOS does not allow: double-clicking a folder in Finder or on the Desktop still opens Finder, and folders can't be reassigned to another app the way documents can — that restriction is Apple's and applies to every file manager, not just Iruka.

Fixed

  • A folder opened inside another one now keeps up with what's on disk. Expanding a folder in place read its contents once and then never looked again, so anything that changed inside it afterwards went unnoticed — drag a file out of an expanded folder and it moved on disk but stayed on screen, and Refresh couldn't clear it either, because Refresh reloads the folder you're in and never reached the rows nested under it. Expanded folders are now watched like any other, so they update on their own, whether the change came from Iruka, from Finder, or from a shell. Closing one and opening it again also re-reads it rather than showing what it looked like last time.
  • Text size now applies to the whole sidebar and to column view. Enlarging the interface text moved Places, Favorites and Volumes but left the section headings, and the SSH, Servers, Cloud and Apps entries, at their old size — and column view ignored the setting entirely. Every one of them scales now, and column rows grow with their text instead of staying a fixed height.
  • The explanations in Settings → Sidebar are readable again. Each one was cut off mid-sentence, and the heading of one group could hang above the rows of the next as you scrolled. They now wrap to as many lines as they need and stay with the group they belong to.
  • Opening Iruka for the first time no longer needs a working internet connection. The notarisation ticket now travels inside the app rather than only on the disk image it came in, so a first launch on a machine that's offline — or behind a strict proxy — no longer risks macOS reporting that it can't check the app for malicious software.

Changed

  • The sidebar fits a third more in the same space. Every row was 32pt tall around 16pt of content, so a sidebar with a few sections' worth of places, favourites and connections ran out of room long before it ran out of screen. Rows are now 24pt, and every section uses the same spacing — places, favourites, apps, volumes and each kind of connection line up with one another instead of drifting apart. Section headings keep a little more room above them, so the groups still read as separate at the tighter spacing. Nothing else about the sidebar changes: the same translucency, the same headings, and the highlight on the folder you're looking at still fills exactly its own row.
